newsitem.title: USA: Carey lead over Hoffa shrinks in Teamster race.
newsitem.headline: Carey lead over Hoffa shrinks in Teamster race.

text.p: Teamsters Union President Ron Carey held onto a slim lead Friday in his re- election bid with nearly two-thirds of the vote tallied, but rival James Hoffa had narrowed the gap considerably.

Court-appointed election officer Barbara Zack Quindel, whose 500-member staff has been tabulating a half-million mail-in ballots since Tuesday, said she expected the count to be finished sometime on Saturday.

But if the winner's victory margin was narrow enough, officials would have to process thousands of uncounted ballots that were set aside for a review of their eligibility -- a painstaking ordeal that could take days.

With 62 percent of the ballots tallied by Friday afternoon, the election officer reported Carey leading Hoffa 52 percent to 48 percent. Carey's vote total was 155,078 compared with Hoffa's 142,379, with 369 of the union's 562 locals counted.
Unofficial tallies from the Carey camp taken at the close of vote-counting late Friday showed him leading Hoffa by 196,656 to 180,565 with 448 locals counted.

Hoffa, son of infamous Teamster leader Jimmy Hoffa, has gained on Carey, who has seen his margin slip from 58 percent on Wednesday to 53 percent on Thursday and 52 percent on Friday, with several big locals in Hoffa's Midwest powerbase untallied.
"The percentages are closing," said Hoffa spokesman Richard Leebove. "We feel we're heading into our strongholds."
Carey spokeswoman Renee Asher said her camp remained "solidly optimistic" about the outcome and noted that several big locals that support Carey also had not been tabulated.

"There was nothing in the numbers that we find discouraging, with the caveat that there are a lot of big locals out there and a lot of them are for Hoffa," she said. "We have some huge locals out there, but so does Hoffa."

The campaign for the leadership of the 1.4 million-member International Brotherhood of Teamsters has been bitter, with each side accusing the other of being corrupt, inept and unfit for a position with a larger constituency than that of any two members of the House of Representatives.
Hoffa, 55, is a Detroit labour lawyer who has worked for the past three years for a Teamster joint council that was once headed by his father.

Carey, 60, won the union's international presidency as a reform candidate five years ago in the union's first government-run election that was open to rank-and-file members. It was required under a 1989 settlement of a federal anti-racketeering lawsuit.

Even if the ballot-counting is finished Saturday, Hoffa backers predicted the margin would be slim enough to require the counting of some of the so-called challenged ballots, those that were set aside for review before being counted.
Quindel reported there were 21,563 challenged ballots on Friday afternoon, more than Carey's margin over Hoffa.
If the winner's victory margin is within 3 percentage points, ballots automatically will be recounted, she said.
She declined to say how long it would take to process challenged ballots or recount all the ballots.
Both candidates positioned themselves for possible post-election challenges by filing protests citing various complaints over election procedures.
